content.prompt: Show that each equation cannot have two real roots.

answer.short: $\alpha^2+\beta^2=(-2)^2-2(5)=-6<0$, so the roots cannot both be real.
answer.worked:
Let the roots be $\alpha$ and $\beta$.
$$\begin{aligned}\alpha+\beta&=-2\\\alpha\beta&=5\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\alpha^2+\beta^2&=(\alpha+\beta)^2-2\alpha\beta\\&=(-2)^2-2(5)\\&=-6<0\end{aligned}$$
If both roots were real, $\alpha^2+\beta^2$ would be non-negative. Therefore the equation cannot have two real roots.

answer.short: $\alpha^2+\beta^2=\left(\dfrac23\right)^2-2\left(\dfrac43\right)=-\dfrac{20}{9}<0$, so the roots cannot both be real.
answer.worked:
Let the roots be $\alpha$ and $\beta$.
$$\begin{aligned}\alpha+\beta&=-\frac{-2}{3}=\frac23\\\alpha\beta&=\frac43\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\alpha^2+\beta^2&=(\alpha+\beta)^2-2\alpha\beta\\&=\left(\frac23\right)^2-2\left(\frac43\right)\\&=\frac49-\frac{24}{9}\\&=-\frac{20}{9}<0\end{aligned}$$
If both roots were real, $\alpha^2+\beta^2$ would be non-negative. Therefore the equation cannot have two real roots.

answer.short: $\alpha^2+\beta^2=0^2-2\left(\dfrac52\right)=-5<0$, so the roots cannot both be real.
answer.worked:
Let the roots be $\alpha$ and $\beta$.
$$\begin{aligned}\alpha+\beta&=-\frac02=0\\\alpha\beta&=\frac52\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\alpha^2+\beta^2&=(\alpha+\beta)^2-2\alpha\beta\\&=0^2-2\left(\frac52\right)\\&=-5<0\end{aligned}$$
If both roots were real, $\alpha^2+\beta^2$ would be non-negative. Therefore the equation cannot have two real roots.

children.prompt: Find $q$ if one root of $x^2-4x+q=0$ is triple the other root.

answer.worked:
Let the roots be $\alpha$ and $3\alpha$.

Sum of roots:
$$\begin{aligned}\alpha+3\alpha&=4\\4\alpha&=4\\\alpha&=1.\end{aligned}$$
The roots are $1$ and $3$.

Product of roots:
$$\begin{aligned}\alpha(3\alpha)&=q\\3\alpha^2&=q\\q&=3(1)^2\\q&=3.\end{aligned}$$

content.prompt: Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be the roots of $2x^2-6x+3=0$. Find the quadratic equation whose roots are:

answer.worked:
$\alpha+\beta=3$, $\alpha\beta=\frac32$.

Let the new quadratic be $x^2+\frac ba x+\frac ca=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}\frac1\alpha+\frac1\beta&=-\frac ba\\\frac{\alpha+\beta}{\alpha\beta}&=-\frac ba\\\frac{3}{3/2}&=-\frac ba\\2&=-\frac ba\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\frac1{\alpha\beta}&=\frac ca\\\frac23&=\frac ca\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}x^2-2x+\frac23&=0\\3x^2-6x+2&=0\end{aligned}$$

$\alpha+\beta=3$, $\alpha\beta=\frac32$.

Let the new quadratic be $x^2+\frac ba x+\frac ca=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}\alpha^2+\beta^2&=-\frac ba\\(\alpha+\beta)^2-2\alpha\beta&=-\frac ba\\3^2-2\left(\frac32\right)&=-\frac ba\\6&=-\frac ba\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\alpha^2\beta^2&=\frac ca\\\left(\frac32\right)^2&=\frac ca\\\frac94&=\frac ca\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}x^2-6x+\frac94&=0\\4x^2-24x+9&=0\end{aligned}$$

$\alpha+\beta=3$, $\alpha\beta=\frac32$.

Let the new quadratic be $x^2+\frac ba x+\frac ca=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}(\alpha-2)+(\beta-2)&=-\frac ba\\\alpha+\beta-4&=-\frac ba\\-1&=-\frac ba\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}(\alpha-2)(\beta-2)&=\frac ca\\\alpha\beta-2(\alpha+\beta)+4&=\frac ca\\\frac32-6+4&=\frac ca\\-\frac12&=\frac ca\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}x^2+x-\frac12&=0\\2x^2+2x-1&=0\end{aligned}$$

(a) Find the value of $\alpha^2+\beta^2$.

answer.short: (a) $-\dfrac74$; (b) The sum of two real squares cannot be negative, but $\alpha^2+\beta^2=-\dfrac74$.
answer.worked:
(a) $\alpha+\beta=\dfrac32$, $\alpha\beta=2$.
$$\begin{aligned}\alpha^2+\beta^2&=(\alpha+\beta)^2-2\alpha\beta\\&=\left(\frac32\right)^2-2(2)\\&=\frac94-4\\&=-\frac74\end{aligned}$$
(b) If both roots were real, $\alpha^2\geq0$ and $\beta^2\geq0$, so their sum would be non-negative. Since $\alpha^2+\beta^2=-\dfrac74$, the roots are not real.

content.prompt: Find the value(s) of $k$ if the quadratic equation $x^2+kx+6=0$ has consecutive roots.

answer.worked:
Let the roots be $r$ and $r+1$.
$$\begin{aligned}r(r+1)&=6\\r^2+r-6&=0\end{aligned}$$
PSF: Product $=-6$, Sum $=1$, Factors $=3$ and $-2$.
$$\begin{aligned}(r+3)(r-2)&=0\\r&=-3\text{ or }2\end{aligned}$$
Sum of roots:
$$\begin{aligned}r+(r+1)&=-k\\2r+1&=-k\end{aligned}$$
When $r=2$: $5=-k$, so $k=-5$.

When $r=-3$: $-5=-k$, so $k=5$.

Hence $k=\pm5$.

content.prompt: Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be the roots of $2x^2-8x+1=0$. Find the quadratic equation whose roots are:

answer.worked:
$\alpha+\beta=4$, $\alpha\beta=\frac12$.

Let the new quadratic be $x^2+\frac{b}{a}x+\frac{c}{a}=0$.

$$\begin{aligned}\frac1\alpha+\frac1\beta&=-\frac ba\\\frac{\beta+\alpha}{\alpha\beta}&=-\frac ba\\\frac{4}{1/2}&=-\frac ba\\8&=-\frac ba\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\frac1{\alpha\beta}&=\frac ca\\\frac1{1/2}&=\frac ca\\2&=\frac ca\end{aligned}$$
Therefore $x^2-8x+2=0$.

$\alpha+\beta=4$, $\alpha\beta=\frac12$.

Let the new quadratic be $x^2+\frac{b}{a}x+\frac{c}{a}=0$.

$$\begin{aligned}\alpha^2+\beta^2&=-\frac ba\\(\alpha+\beta)^2-2\alpha\beta&=-\frac ba\\4^2-1&=-\frac ba\\15&=-\frac ba\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\alpha^2\beta^2&=\frac ca\\\left(\frac12\right)^2&=\frac ca\\\frac14&=\frac ca\end{aligned}$$
The equation is $x^2-15x+\frac14=0$.

Therefore $4x^2-60x+1=0$.

content.prompt:
Let the roots of $x^2-3x+10=0$ be $\alpha$ and $\beta$.

answer.worked:
$\alpha+\beta=3$, $\alpha\beta=10$.

Let the new quadratic be $x^2+\frac{b}{a}x+\frac{c}{a}=0$.

Sum of roots:
$$\begin{aligned}(\alpha+2)+(\beta+2)&=-\frac{b}{a}\\\alpha+\beta+4&=-\frac{b}{a}\\7&=-\frac{b}{a}\end{aligned}$$
Product of roots:
$$\begin{aligned}(\alpha+2)(\beta+2)&=\frac{c}{a}\\\alpha\beta+2(\alpha+\beta)+4&=\frac{c}{a}\\10+2(3)+4&=\frac{c}{a}\\20&=\frac{c}{a}\end{aligned}$$
Therefore $x^2-7x+20=0$.

sourceAtom.label: Sum and product of zeroes for a cubic equation

inlines.text: . Suppose the monic polynomial can be factorised as
, equate coefficients to determine the relationship between zeroes and coefficients.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}P(x)&=(x-\alpha)(x-\beta)(x-\gamma)\\&=\bigl(x^2-(\alpha+\beta)x+\alpha\beta\bigr)(x-\gamma)\\&=x^3-\gamma x^2-(\alpha+\beta)x^2+(\alpha+\beta)\gamma x+\alpha\beta x-\alpha\beta\gamma\\&=x^3-(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)x^2+(\alpha\beta+\alpha\gamma+\beta\gamma)x-\alpha\beta\gamma.\end{aligned}$$
Equating coefficients with $P(x)=x^3+\dfrac{b}{a}x^2+\dfrac{c}{a}x+\dfrac{d}{a}$ gives
$$\begin{aligned}-(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)&=\frac{b}{a},\\\alpha\beta+\alpha\gamma+\beta\gamma&=\frac{c}{a},\\-\alpha\beta\gamma&=\frac{d}{a}.\end{aligned}$$
Hence $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=-\dfrac{b}{a}$, $\alpha\beta+\alpha\gamma+\beta\gamma=\dfrac{c}{a}$ and $\alpha\beta\gamma=-\dfrac{d}{a}$.

sourceReview.taughtMethod: Expand the three linear factors of the monic cubic, collect like terms and equate coefficients.

blocks.title: Sum and product of zeroes (cubic)
blocks.content:
For a cubic $P(x)=ax^3+bx^2+cx+d$, with $a\ne0$ and the three zeroes $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ (real or non-real, a repeated zero counted by its multiplicity):
$$\begin{aligned}\alpha+\beta+\gamma&=-\frac{b}{a}\\\alpha\beta+\alpha\gamma+\beta\gamma&=\frac{c}{a}\\\alpha\beta\gamma&=-\frac{d}{a}\end{aligned}$$
Describe $\alpha\beta+\alpha\gamma+\beta\gamma$ as “sum of products taken two at a time”.

content.prompt: Complete the following.

children.label: a
children.prompt:
Let $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ be the roots of $x^3+3x^2-6x-2=0$.
Find the cubic equation whose roots are $-2\alpha,-2\beta$ and $-2\gamma$.

answer.worked:
For the original roots,
$$\begin{align*}\alpha+\beta+\gamma&=-3\\\alpha\beta+\alpha\gamma+\beta\gamma&=-6\\\alpha\beta\gamma&=2.\end{align*}$$
For the new roots $-2\alpha,-2\beta,-2\gamma$,
$$\begin{align*}-2(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)&=-2(-3)=6,\\4(\alpha\beta+\alpha\gamma+\beta\gamma)&=4(-6)=-24,\\-8\alpha\beta\gamma&=-8(2)=-16.\end{align*}$$
The required equation is
$$\begin{align*}x^3-6x^2+(-24)x-(-16)&=0\\x^3-6x^2-24x+16&=0.\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt:
Let $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ be the roots of $2x^3-4x^2+5x+1=0$.
Find the cubic equation whose roots are $\frac1\alpha,\frac1\beta,\frac1\gamma$.

answer.worked:
For the original roots,
$$\begin{align*}\alpha+\beta+\gamma&=2\\\alpha\beta+\alpha\gamma+\beta\gamma&=\frac52\\\alpha\beta\gamma&=-\frac12.\end{align*}$$
For the new roots $\frac1\alpha,\frac1\beta,\frac1\gamma$,
$$\begin{align*}\frac1\alpha+\frac1\beta+\frac1\gamma&=\frac{\alpha\beta+\alpha\gamma+\beta\gamma}{\alpha\beta\gamma}=\frac{5/2}{-1/2}=-5,\\\frac1{\alpha\beta}+\frac1{\alpha\gamma}+\frac1{\beta\gamma}&=\frac{\alpha+\beta+\gamma}{\alpha\beta\gamma}=\frac{2}{-1/2}=-4,\\\frac1{\alpha\beta\gamma}&=\frac1{-1/2}=-2.\end{align*}$$
The required equation is
$$\begin{align*}x^3-(-5)x^2+(-4)x-(-2)&=0\\x^3+5x^2-4x+2&=0.\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt:
Let $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ be the roots of $x^3-4x+6=0$.
Find the cubic equation whose roots are $\frac1\alpha,\frac1\beta,\frac1\gamma$.

answer.worked:
For the original roots,
$$\begin{align*}\alpha+\beta+\gamma&=0\\\alpha\beta+\alpha\gamma+\beta\gamma&=-4\\\alpha\beta\gamma&=-6.\end{align*}$$
For the new roots $\frac1\alpha,\frac1\beta,\frac1\gamma$,
$$\begin{align*}\frac1\alpha+\frac1\beta+\frac1\gamma&=\frac{-4}{-6}=\frac23,\\\frac1{\alpha\beta}+\frac1{\alpha\gamma}+\frac1{\beta\gamma}&=\frac{0}{-6}=0,\\\frac1{\alpha\beta\gamma}&=\frac1{-6}=-\frac16.\end{align*}$$
The required equation is
$$\begin{align*}x^3-\frac23x^2+0x+\frac16&=0\\\color{#ef6068}{6\times}\left(x^3-\frac23x^2+\frac16\right)&=\color{#ef6068}{6\times}\,0\\6x^3-4x^2+1&=0.\end{align*}$$

children.label: a
children.prompt: If two zeroes of the cubic $f(x)=ax^3+bx^2+cx+d$ are opposites, prove that $ad=bc$.

answer.short: Writing the zeroes as $t,-t,u$ gives $b=-au$, $c=-at^2$ and $d=at^2u$, so $ad=bc=a^2t^2u$.
answer.worked:
Let the zeroes be $t,-t,u$. Since $f$ is cubic, $a\ne0$. Using the sums and products of zeroes:
$$\begin{aligned}t-t+u&=-\frac ba\\u&=-\frac ba\\t(-t)+tu+(-t)u&=\frac ca\\-t^2&=\frac ca\\t(-t)u&=-\frac da\\t^2u&=\frac da.\end{aligned}$$
Hence
$$\begin{aligned}bc&=(-au)(-at^2)\\bc&=a^2t^2u\\ad&=a(at^2u)\\ad&=a^2t^2u.\end{aligned}$$
Therefore $ad=bc$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: If two of the roots of the equation $x^3+qx+r=0$ are equal, show that $4q^3+27r^2=0$.

answer.short: Let the roots be $t,t,-2t$. Then $q=-3t^2$ and $r=2t^3$, giving $4q^3+27r^2=-108t^6+108t^6=0$.
answer.worked:
Let the roots be $t,t,u$. Using the sum of roots:
$$\begin{aligned}t+t+u&=0\\u&=-2t.\end{aligned}$$
Using the sum of products taken two at a time and the product of roots:
$$\begin{aligned}q&=t^2+t(-2t)+t(-2t)\\q&=-3t^2\\-r&=t\cdot t\cdot(-2t)\\r&=2t^3.\end{aligned}$$
Therefore
$$\begin{aligned}4q^3+27r^2&=4(-3t^2)^3+27(2t^3)^2\\4q^3+27r^2&=-108t^6+108t^6\\4q^3+27r^2&=0.\end{aligned}$$

children.label: a
children.prompt: The polynomial $P(x)=2x^3-5x^2-14x+8$ has zeroes at $-2$ and $4$. Use the sum of zeroes to find the other zero.

answer.worked:
Let the other zero be $\gamma$. Using the sum of zeroes,
$$\begin{aligned}-2+4+\gamma&=\frac52\\\gamma&=\frac52-2\\&=\frac12.\end{aligned}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Suppose that $x-3$ and $x+1$ are factors of $P(x)=x^3-6x^2+5x+12$. Use the product of the zeroes to find the other factor of $P(x)$.

answer.worked:
Two zeroes are $3$ and $-1$. Let the other zero be $\gamma$. Using the product of zeroes,
$$\begin{aligned}(3)(-1)\gamma&=-12\\\gamma&=4.\end{aligned}$$
The other factor is $x-4$.

content.prompt:
Let $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ be the roots of $x^3+4x^2-5x-2=0$.
Find the cubic equation whose roots are $3\alpha,3\beta$, and $3\gamma$.

answer.worked:
For the original roots,
$$\begin{align*}
\alpha+\beta+\gamma&=-4\\
\alpha\beta+\alpha\gamma+\beta\gamma&=-5\\
\alpha\beta\gamma&=2.
\end{align*}$$
For the new roots $3\alpha,3\beta,3\gamma$,
$$\begin{align*}
3\alpha+3\beta+3\gamma&=3(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)\\
&=3(-4)\\
&=-12,\\
(3\alpha)(3\beta)+(3\alpha)(3\gamma)+(3\beta)(3\gamma)&=9\alpha\beta+9\alpha\gamma+9\beta\gamma\\
&=9(\alpha\beta+\alpha\gamma+\beta\gamma)\\
&=9(-5)\\
&=-45,\\
(3\alpha)(3\beta)(3\gamma)&=27\alpha\beta\gamma\\
&=27(2)\\
&=54.
\end{align*}$$
A monic cubic with root sum $S_1$, sum of pairwise products $S_2$ and root product $S_3$ has equation $x^3-S_1x^2+S_2x-S_3=0$. Therefore the required equation is
$$x^3+12x^2-45x-54=0.$$

content.prompt: Show that $x=1$ and $x=-2$ are zeroes of $P(x)$, and use the sum or product of zeroes to find the other zero.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}P(1)&=1-2-5+6\\&=0\\P(-2)&=-8-8+10+6\\&=0\end{align*}$$
Thus $1$ and $-2$ are zeroes. Let the other zero be $\gamma$. Using the sum of roots,
$$\begin{align*}1-2+\gamma&=-\frac{-2}{1}\\\gamma&=3.\end{align*}$$

$$\begin{align*}P(1)&=2+3-3-2\\&=0\\P(-2)&=-16+12+6-2\\&=0\end{align*}$$
Thus $1$ and $-2$ are zeroes. Let the other zero be $\gamma$. Using the sum of roots,
$$\begin{align*}1-2+\gamma&=-\frac32\\\gamma&=-\frac12.\end{align*}$$

children.prompt: Write down the corresponding linear factor, then completely factorise $x^3-3x^2-x+3=0$.

answer.worked:
Since 1 is a root, $x-1$ is a linear factor. Long division gives
$$\begin{array}{r|rrrr} &x^2-2x-3&&&\\x-1&x^3&-3x^2&-x&+3\\ &x^3&-x^2&&\\\hline &&-2x^2&-x&\\ &&-2x^2&+2x&\\\hline &&&-3x&+3\\ &&&-3x&+3\\\hline &&&&0\end{array}$$
$$\begin{aligned}x^3-3x^2-x+3&=(x-1)(x^2-2x-3)\\&=(x-1)(x-3)(x+1)\end{aligned}$$
Hence the equation is $(x-1)(x-3)(x+1)=0$.

content.prompt:
Find the roots of $3x^3-8x^2-5x+6=0$ given that the product of two of them is 2.

Hint: let the roots be $\alpha,\dfrac2\alpha,\beta$

answer.worked:
Let the roots be $\alpha,\dfrac2\alpha,\beta$.

Sum of roots:
$$\alpha+\frac2\alpha+\beta=\frac83\qquad(1)$$
Product of roots:
$$\begin{aligned}\alpha\left(\frac2\alpha\right)\beta&=-\frac63\\2\beta&=-2\\\beta&=-1.\end{aligned}$$
Substituting $\beta=-1$ into (1):
$$\begin{aligned}\alpha+\frac2\alpha-1&=\frac83\\\alpha+\frac2\alpha&=\frac{11}{3}\\3\alpha^2-11\alpha+6&=0\end{aligned}$$
PSF (Product, Sum, Factors): Product $=3\times6=18$, Sum $=-11$, Factors: $-9$ and $-2$.
$$\begin{aligned}3\alpha^2-9\alpha-2\alpha+6&=0\\3\alpha(\alpha-3)-2(\alpha-3)&=0\\(3\alpha-2)(\alpha-3)&=0.\end{aligned}$$
If $\alpha=3$, then $\dfrac2\alpha=\dfrac23$; if $\alpha=\dfrac23$, then $\dfrac2\alpha=3$.

Therefore $x=3,\dfrac23,-1$.

content.prompt: Find the roots of $x^3+3x^2-13x-15=0$, given that the roots are in arithmetic progression.

answer.worked:
Let the roots be $\alpha-d,\alpha,\alpha+d$.

Using the sum of roots:
$$\begin{aligned}3\alpha&=-3\\\alpha&=-1\end{aligned}$$
Using the product of roots:
$$\begin{aligned}(-1-d)(-1)(-1+d)&=15\\d^2-1&=15\\d^2&=16\\d&=\pm4\end{aligned}$$
Hence $x=-5,-1,3$.

content.prompt:
Let $x^3-2x^2+3x-1=0$ have roots $\alpha$, $\beta$ and $\gamma$.

(a) Find the value of $\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2$.

(b) Hence, explain why the graph of $y=x^3-2x^2+3x-1$ cannot have 3 $x$-intercepts.

answer.short: (a) $-2$. (b) If all three roots were real, the sum of their squares would be non-negative. Since the sum is $-2$, the roots cannot all be real, so the graph cannot have 3 $x$-intercepts.
answer.worked:
(a)
$$\begin{aligned}\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2&=(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)^2-2(\alpha\beta+\alpha\gamma+\beta\gamma)\\&=2^2-2(3)\\&=-2\end{aligned}$$
(b) A cubic has three roots, counting multiplicity. If all three were real, $\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2\geq0$. Part a gives $\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2=-2$, so the roots cannot all be real. Hence the graph cannot have 3 $x$-intercepts.

content.prompt: Two roots of the cubic equation $x^3+ax^2+bx+24=0$ are $4$ and $-2$. Find the values of $a$ and $b$ and hence state the equation of the cubic.

answer.worked:
Let the third root be $\gamma$. Using the product of roots,
$$\begin{aligned}(4)(-2)\gamma&=-24\\\gamma&=3.\end{aligned}$$
Using the sum of roots,
$$\begin{aligned}4-2+3&=-a\\a&=-5.\end{aligned}$$
Using the sum of products taken two at a time,
$$\begin{aligned}b&=(4)(-2)+(4)(3)+(-2)(3)\\&=-8+12-6\\&=-2.\end{aligned}$$
Hence the cubic equation is $x^3-5x^2-2x+24=0$.

content.prompt:
Consider $P(x)=x^3-3x^2+7x-5$.

(a) Show that $1$ is a zero of $P(x)$.

(b) Suppose that the zeroes of $P(x)$ are $1$, $\alpha$ and $\beta$. Show that $\alpha+\beta=2$ and $\alpha\beta=5$.

(c) By solving the two equations in part b simultaneously, show that $\alpha^2-2\alpha+5=0$.

(d) Hence show there are no such real numbers $\alpha$ and $\beta$.

(e) Hence state how many times the graph of $P(x)$ crosses the $x$-axis.

answer.worked:
(a)
$$\begin{aligned}P(1)&=1^3-3(1)^2+7(1)-5\\&=1-3+7-5\\&=0\end{aligned}$$
Therefore $1$ is a zero of $P(x)$.

(b) Using the sum of zeroes,
$$\begin{aligned}1+\alpha+\beta&=3\\\alpha+\beta&=2.\end{aligned}$$
Using the product of zeroes,
$$\begin{aligned}1\cdot\alpha\beta&=5\\\alpha\beta&=5.\end{aligned}$$
(c) From part b, $\beta=2-\alpha$. Substitute into $\alpha\beta=5$:
$$\begin{aligned}\alpha(2-\alpha)&=5\\2\alpha-\alpha^2&=5\\\alpha^2-2\alpha+5&=0.\end{aligned}$$
(d)
$$\begin{aligned}\Delta&=(-2)^2-4(1)(5)\\&=-16<0.\end{aligned}$$
Thus $\alpha$ is not real. Since $\beta=2-\alpha$, $\beta$ is not real either.

(e) The only real zero is $1$, and it is a simple zero. Therefore the graph crosses the $x$-axis once.

content.prompt:
Consider $P(x)=x^3-2x^2+x+4$.

(a) Show that $-1$ is a zero of $P(x)$.

(b) Suppose that the zeroes of $P(x)$ are $-1$, $\alpha$ and $\beta$. Show that $\alpha+\beta=3$ and $\alpha\beta=4$.

(c) By solving the two equations in part b simultaneously, show that $\alpha^2-3\alpha+4=0$.

(d) Hence show there are no such real numbers $\alpha$ and $\beta$.

(e) Hence state how many times the graph of $P(x)$ crosses the $x$-axis.

answer.worked:
(a)
$$\begin{aligned}P(-1)&=(-1)^3-2(-1)^2+(-1)+4\\&=-1-2-1+4\\&=0\end{aligned}$$
Therefore $-1$ is a zero of $P(x)$.

(b) Using the sum of zeroes,
$$\begin{aligned}\alpha+\beta-1&=2\\\alpha+\beta&=3.\end{aligned}$$
Using the product of zeroes,
$$\begin{aligned}-\alpha\beta&=-4\\\alpha\beta&=4.\end{aligned}$$
(c) From part b, $\beta=3-\alpha$. Substitute into $\alpha\beta=4$:
$$\begin{aligned}\alpha(3-\alpha)&=4\\3\alpha-\alpha^2&=4\\\alpha^2-3\alpha+4&=0.\end{aligned}$$
(d)
$$\begin{aligned}\Delta&=(-3)^2-4(1)(4)\\&=-7<0.\end{aligned}$$

children.label: a
children.prompt:
Let $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ be the roots of $2x^3-4x^2+3x-1=0$.
Find the cubic equation whose roots are $2\alpha,2\beta$, and $2\gamma$.

answer.worked:
For the original roots,
$$\begin{align*}
\alpha+\beta+\gamma&=2\\
\alpha\beta+\alpha\gamma+\beta\gamma&=\frac32\\
\alpha\beta\gamma&=\frac12.
\end{align*}$$
For the new roots $2\alpha,2\beta,2\gamma$,
$$\begin{align*}
2\alpha+2\beta+2\gamma&=2(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)\\
&=2(2)\\
&=4,\\
(2\alpha)(2\beta)+(2\alpha)(2\gamma)+(2\beta)(2\gamma)&=4\alpha\beta+4\alpha\gamma+4\beta\gamma\\
&=4(\alpha\beta+\alpha\gamma+\beta\gamma)\\
&=4\left(\frac32\right)\\
&=6,\\
(2\alpha)(2\beta)(2\gamma)&=8\alpha\beta\gamma\\
&=8\left(\frac12\right)\\
&=4.
\end{align*}$$
A monic cubic with root sum $S_1$, sum of pairwise products $S_2$ and root product $S_3$ has equation $x^3-S_1x^2+S_2x-S_3=0$. Therefore the required equation is
$$x^3-4x^2+6x-4=0.$$

children.label: b
children.prompt:
Let $x^3-3x^2+5x+2=0$ have zeroes $\alpha,\beta$, and $\gamma$.
Find a polynomial equation with roots $\frac1\alpha,\frac1\beta,\frac1\gamma$.

answer.worked:
For the original roots,
$$\begin{align*}
\alpha+\beta+\gamma&=3\\
\alpha\beta+\alpha\gamma+\beta\gamma&=5\\
\alpha\beta\gamma&=-2.
\end{align*}$$
For the new roots $\frac1\alpha,\frac1\beta,\frac1\gamma$,
$$\begin{align*}
\frac1\alpha+\frac1\beta+\frac1\gamma&=\frac{\beta\gamma+\alpha\gamma+\alpha\beta}{\alpha\beta\gamma}\\
&=\frac5{-2}\\
&=-\frac52,\\
\left(\frac1\alpha\right)\left(\frac1\beta\right)+\left(\frac1\alpha\right)\left(\frac1\gamma\right)+\left(\frac1\beta\right)\left(\frac1\gamma\right)&=\frac1{\alpha\beta}+\frac1{\alpha\gamma}+\frac1{\beta\gamma}\\
&=\frac{\gamma+\beta+\alpha}{\alpha\beta\gamma}\\
&=\frac3{-2}\\
&=-\frac32,\\
\left(\frac1\alpha\right)\left(\frac1\beta\right)\left(\frac1\gamma\right)&=\frac1{\alpha\beta\gamma}\\
&=\frac1{-2}\\
&=-\frac12.
\end{align*}$$
The required equation is
$$\begin{align*}
x^3-\left(-\frac52\right)x^2-\frac32x-\left(-\frac12\right)&=0\\

\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: The cubic equation $x^3-Ax^2+3A=0$, where $A>0$, has roots $\alpha$, $\beta$, and $\alpha+\beta$. Show that $A=2\sqrt6$.

answer.short: $\alpha+\beta=\dfrac A2$ and $\alpha\beta=-\dfrac{A^2}{4}$. The product of roots gives $-\dfrac{A^3}{8}=-3A$, so $A^2=24$. Since $A>0$, $A=2\sqrt6$.
answer.worked:
Sum of roots:
$$2\alpha+2\beta=A\qquad(1)$$
Sum of products of pairs of roots:
$$\alpha\beta+\beta(\alpha+\beta)+\alpha(\alpha+\beta)=0\qquad(2)$$
Product of roots:
$$\alpha\beta(\alpha+\beta)=-3A\qquad(3)$$
Rearranging (1) gives $\alpha+\beta=\dfrac A2$. Substituting into (2),
$$\begin{aligned}\alpha\beta+\beta\left(\frac A2\right)+\alpha\left(\frac A2\right)&=0\\\alpha\beta+\frac A2(\alpha+\beta)&=0\\\alpha\beta+\frac{A^2}{4}&=0\\\alpha\beta&=-\frac{A^2}{4}.\end{aligned}$$
Substituting $\alpha+\beta$ and $\alpha\beta$ into (3),
$$\begin{aligned}-\frac{A^2}{4}\left(\frac A2\right)&=-3A\\-\frac{A^3}{8}&=-3A\\A^2&=24,\end{aligned}$$
where division by $A$ is valid because $A>0$. Taking the positive root,
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\sqrt{24}\\&=2\sqrt6.\end{aligned}$$

content.prompt: Find the values of $a$ and $b$ for which $x^3+ax^2-10x+b$ is exactly divisible by $x^2+x-12$, and then factor the cubic.

answer.worked:
Let $P(x)=x^3+ax^2-10x+b$.
$$\begin{align*}x^2+x-12&=(x-3)(x+4)\\P(3)&=0\\27+9a-30+b&=0\\9a+b&=3\\P(-4)&=0\\-64+16a+40+b&=0\\16a+b&=24\end{align*}$$
Solving simultaneously,
$$\begin{align*}7a&=21\\a&=3\\b&=-24.\end{align*}$$
Thus the cubic is $x^3+3x^2-10x-24$. From here, use either long division or the sum of roots to find the third root. Using the sum of roots, with third root $r$:
$$\begin{align*}3+(-4)+r&=-3\\r&=-2\\x^3+3x^2-10x-24&=(x-3)(x+4)(x+2).\end{align*}$$

For a quartic $P(x)=ax^4+bx^3+cx^2+dx+e$, where $a\ne0$ and $\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta$ are its four zeroes (real or non-real, a repeated zero counted by its multiplicity):
$$\begin{aligned}\alpha+\beta+\gamma+\delta&=-\frac{b}{a}\\\alpha\beta+\alpha\gamma+\alpha\delta+\beta\gamma+\beta\delta+\gamma\delta&=\frac{c}{a}\\\alpha\beta\gamma+\alpha\beta\delta+\alpha\gamma\delta+\beta\gamma\delta&=-\frac{d}{a}\\\alpha\beta\gamma\delta&=\frac{e}{a}\end{aligned}$$
All methods in the previous sections apply.

content.prompt: Complete the following.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Show that $x^4+2x^3+4x^2-x+5=0$ cannot have four real roots.

answer.short: The sum of the squares of the roots is $(-2)^2-2(4)=-4<0$, which is impossible if all four roots are real.
answer.worked:
Let the roots be $\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta$.
$$\begin{aligned}\alpha+\beta+\gamma+\delta&=-2\\\alpha\beta+\alpha\gamma+\alpha\delta+\beta\gamma+\beta\delta+\gamma\delta&=4\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2+\delta^2&=(\alpha+\beta+\gamma+\delta)^2\\&\quad-2(\alpha\beta+\alpha\gamma+\alpha\delta+\beta\gamma+\beta\delta+\gamma\delta)\\&=(-2)^2-2(4)\\&=-4<0\end{aligned}$$
If all four roots were real, each square would be non-negative, so their sum would be non-negative. Therefore the equation cannot have four real roots.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Show that $3x^4-6x^3+7x^2+2x-8=0$ cannot have four real roots.

answer.short: The sum of the squares of the roots is $2^2-2\left(\dfrac73\right)=-\dfrac23<0$, which is impossible if all four roots are real.
answer.worked:
Let the roots be $\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta$.
$$\begin{aligned}\alpha+\beta+\gamma+\delta&=-\frac{-6}{3}=2\\\alpha\beta+\alpha\gamma+\alpha\delta+\beta\gamma+\beta\delta+\gamma\delta&=\frac73\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2+\delta^2&=(\alpha+\beta+\gamma+\delta)^2\\&\quad-2(\alpha\beta+\alpha\gamma+\alpha\delta+\beta\gamma+\beta\delta+\gamma\delta)\\&=2^2-2\left(\frac73\right)\\&=-\frac23<0\end{aligned}$$
If all four roots were real, each square would be non-negative, so their sum would be non-negative. Therefore the equation cannot have four real roots.

content.prompt: Show that $x=1$ and $x=-2$ are zeroes of $P(x)$, then find the other two zeroes using sum and product of roots.

answer.short: $P(1)=P(-2)=0$; the other zeroes are $-3$ and $1$, so $1$ is a double zero.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}P(1)&=1+3-3-7+6\\P(1)&=0,\\P(-2)&=16-24-12+14+6\\P(-2)&=0.\end{aligned}$$
Thus $1$ and $-2$ are zeroes. Let the other zeroes be $\alpha,\beta$.

Using the sum of roots,
$$\begin{aligned}\alpha+\beta-2+1&=-3\\\alpha+\beta&=-2.\end{aligned}$$
Using the product of roots,
$$\begin{aligned}-2\alpha\beta&=6\\\alpha\beta&=-3.\end{aligned}$$
Solving simultaneously,
$$\begin{aligned}\alpha(-2-\alpha)&=-3\\\alpha^2+2\alpha-3&=0\\(\alpha+3)(\alpha-1)&=0.\end{aligned}$$
If $\alpha=-3$, then $\beta=1$; if $\alpha=1$, then $\beta=-3$. The other zeroes are $-3$ and $1$, so $1$ is a double zero.

$$\begin{aligned}P(1)&=3-5-10+20-8\\P(1)&=0,\\P(-2)&=48+40-40-40-8\\P(-2)&=0.\end{aligned}$$
Thus $1$ and $-2$ are zeroes. Let the other zeroes be $\alpha,\beta$.

Using the sum of roots,
$$\begin{aligned}\alpha+\beta-2+1&=\frac53\\\alpha+\beta&=\frac83.\end{aligned}$$
Using the product of roots,
$$\begin{aligned}-2\alpha\beta&=-\frac83\\\alpha\beta&=\frac43.\end{aligned}$$
Solving simultaneously,
$$\begin{aligned}\alpha\left(\frac83-\alpha\right)&=\frac43\\3\alpha^2-8\alpha+4&=0\\(3\alpha-2)(\alpha-2)&=0.\end{aligned}$$
If $\alpha=\dfrac23$, then $\beta=2$; if $\alpha=2$, then $\beta=\dfrac23$. The other zeroes are $\dfrac23$ and $2$.

content.prompt: Complete the following.

children.label: a
children.prompt: The polynomial $P(x)=x^4+ax^3+bx^2+cx+d$ has two zeroes that are opposites. Show that $a^2d+c^2=abc$.

answer.short: Taking the zeroes as $t,-t,u,v$, the sum and triple-product relations give $c=-at^2$, and the pair and product relations give $d=-t^2(b+t^2)$. Eliminating $t^2$ gives $a^2d+c^2=abc$.
answer.worked:
Let the zeroes be $t,-t,u,v$.

Sum of roots:
$$u+v=-a\qquad(1)$$
Sum of products two at a time:
$$\begin{align*}-t^2+tu+tv-tu-tv+uv&=b\\uv-t^2&=b\qquad(2)\end{align*}$$
Sum of products three at a time:
$$\begin{align*}-t^2u-t^2v+tuv-tuv&=-c\\-t^2(u+v)&=-c\qquad(3)\end{align*}$$
Product of roots:
$$-t^2uv=d\qquad(4)$$
Substitute (1) into (3):
$$\begin{align*}-t^2(-a)&=-c\\c&=-at^2\qquad(5)\end{align*}$$
Substitute (2) into (4):
$$\begin{align*}d&=-t^2(b+t^2)\\a^2d&=-a^2bt^2-a^2t^4\qquad(6)\end{align*}$$
From (5), $c^2=a^2t^4$ and $abc=-a^2bt^2$. Add $c^2$ to (6):
$$\begin{align*}a^2d+c^2&=-a^2bt^2\\&=abc.\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: The polynomial equation $x^4+px^3+qx^2+rx+s=0$ has two pairs of equal roots. Show that $p^3-4pq+8r=0$.

answer.short: Taking the roots as $t,t,u,u$, the sum and pair relations give $tu=\dfrac{4q-p^2}{8}$, and the triple relation gives $r=p\,tu$. Eliminating $tu$ gives $p^3-4pq+8r=0$.
answer.worked:
Let the roots be $t,t,u,u$.

Sum of roots:
$$\begin{align*}2t+2u&=-p\\t+u&=-\frac p2\qquad(1)\end{align*}$$
Sum of products two at a time:
$$\begin{align*}t^2+4tu+u^2&=q\\(t+u)^2+2tu&=q\qquad(2)\end{align*}$$
Sum of products three at a time:
$$\begin{align*}2t^2u+2tu^2&=-r\\2tu(t+u)&=-r\qquad(3)\end{align*}$$
Substitute (1) into (2):
$$\begin{align*}\frac{p^2}{4}+2tu&=q\\tu&=\frac{4q-p^2}{8}\qquad(4)\end{align*}$$
Substitute (1) into (3):
$$\begin{align*}2tu\left(-\frac p2\right)&=-r\\r&=p\,tu\qquad(5)\end{align*}$$
Substitute (4) into (5):
$$\begin{align*}r&=\frac{p(4q-p^2)}{8}\\8r&=4pq-p^3\\p^3-4pq+8r&=0.\end{align*}$$

content.prompt:
Find the points of intersection of a cubic and a line.

Consider $y=4-x$ and $y=x^3-5x^2+6x+1$.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Equate the two curves to find an equation that can be used to find the points of intersection.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Find two roots using factor theorem, then use sum of roots to find the third root.

answer.short: The roots are $1$, $3$ and $1$; $1$ is a double root.
answer.worked:
Let $P(x)=x^3-5x^2+7x-3$.

$$\begin{aligned}P(1)&=1-5+7-3\\&=0\\P(3)&=27-45+21-3\\&=0\end{aligned}$$

By the factor theorem, $1$ and $3$ are roots. If the third root is $r$, the sum of roots gives

$$\begin{aligned}1+3+r&=5\\r&=1\end{aligned}$$

Thus the roots are $1$, $1$ and $3$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Hence explain why the line is tangent to the cubic, and state the points of intersection.

answer.short: The double root $x=1$ means the line is tangent to the cubic at $(1,3)$. The intersections are $(1,3)$ and $(3,1)$.

$$x^3-5x^2+7x-3=(x-1)^2(x-3).$$

The double root $x=1$ means the curves touch without crossing there, so the line is tangent to the cubic.

Using $y=4-x$:

$$\begin{aligned}x=1:\quad y&=4-1=3\\x=3:\quad y&=4-3=1\end{aligned}$$

The points of intersection are $(1,3)$ and $(3,1)$.

answer.worked:

(b) PSF: Product $4$, Sum $4$, Factors $2$ and $2$.

content.prompt:
Consider the line $y=2x+k$ and the parabola $y=x^2-4x$.

(a) Show that the $x$-coordinates of the points of intersection satisfy the equation
$$x^2-6x-k=0.$$

(b) Suppose that the line is a tangent to the parabola; in other words, the two roots of the quadratic equation are equal. Let the roots be $\alpha$ and $\alpha$.

(i) Using sum of roots, show that $\alpha=3$.

(ii) Using product of roots, show that $\alpha^2=-k$ and hence find $k$.

(iii) Therefore, state the equation of the tangent line and find its point of contact with the parabola.

answer.short: $x^2-6x-k=0$; $\alpha=3$; $\alpha^2=-k$, so $k=-9$. Tangent line: $y=2x-9$. Point of contact: $(3,-3)$.
answer.worked:
(a)
$$\begin{aligned}2x+k&=x^2-4x\\x^2-6x-k&=0\end{aligned}$$
(b)(i)
$$\begin{aligned}\alpha+\alpha&=-\frac{b}{a}\\2\alpha&=-\frac{-6}{1}\\2\alpha&=6\\\alpha&=3\end{aligned}$$
(ii)
$$\begin{aligned}\alpha\times\alpha&=\frac{c}{a}\\\alpha^2&=-k\\3^2&=-k\\k&=-9\end{aligned}$$
(iii) The tangent line is $y=2x-9$.
At the point of contact, PSF: Product $9$, Sum $-6$, Factors $-3$ and $-3$.

content.prompt: The line $y=mx-4$ meets the parabola $y=x^2-3x$ at $A$ and $B$. The midpoint $M$ of $AB$ has $x$-coordinate $3$, as shown. Find $m$.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}x^2-3x&=mx-4\\x^2-(3+m)x+4&=0\end{align*}$$
Let the $x$-coordinates of $A$ and $B$ be $\alpha$ and $\beta$.
$$\begin{align*}\alpha+\beta&=-\frac ba\\&=3+m\end{align*}$$
The $x$-coordinate of $M$ is the average of $\alpha$ and $\beta$.
$$\begin{align*}\frac{\alpha+\beta}{2}&=3\\\alpha+\beta&=6\\3+m&=6\\m&=3\end{align*}$$

content.prompt:
The line $y=3x-6$ meets the cubic $y=x^3-6x^2+8x$ at $F(2,0)$ and also at points $A$ and $B$. Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be the $x$-coordinates of $A$ and $B$, respectively.

(a) Show that $\alpha$ and $\beta$ satisfy $x^3-6x^2+5x+6=0$.

(b) Find $\alpha+\beta$.

(c) Show that $\alpha\beta=-3$.

(d) Use the identity $(\alpha-\beta)^2=(\alpha+\beta)^2-4\alpha\beta$ to show that the horizontal distance $|\alpha-\beta|$ between $A$ and $B$ is $2\sqrt{7}$.

(e) Hence find the exact length of $AB$ using the horizontal distance and the gradient.

answer.worked:
(a)
$$\begin{aligned}x^3-6x^2+8x&=3x-6\\x^3-6x^2+5x+6&=0\end{aligned}$$
(b) The third root is $2$, from $F(2,0)$. Using the sum of roots,
$$\begin{aligned}\alpha+\beta+2&=6\\\alpha+\beta&=4\end{aligned}$$
(c) Using the product of the three roots,
$$\begin{aligned}\alpha\beta(2)&=-\frac{6}{1}\\\alpha\beta&=-3\end{aligned}$$
(d)
$$\begin{aligned}(\alpha-\beta)^2&=(\alpha+\beta)^2-4\alpha\beta\\&=4^2-4(-3)\\&=28\\|\alpha-\beta|&=\sqrt{28}\\&=2\sqrt{7}\end{aligned}$$
(e) The gradient is $3$, so the vertical distance is $3(2\sqrt{7})=6\sqrt{7}$. By Pythagoras,
$$\begin{aligned}AB&=\sqrt{(2\sqrt{7})^2+(6\sqrt{7})^2}\\&=\sqrt{28+252}\\&=\sqrt{280}\\&=2\sqrt{70}\end{aligned}$$

(b) The third root is $-1$, from $F(-1,0)$. Using the sum of roots,
$$\begin{aligned}\alpha+\beta+(-1)&=2\\\alpha+\beta&=3\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}\alpha\beta(-1)&=-\frac{-2}{1}\\-\alpha\beta&=2\\\alpha\beta&=-2\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}(\alpha-\beta)^2&=(\alpha+\beta)^2-4\alpha\beta\\&=3^2-4(-2)\\&=17\\|\alpha-\beta|&=\sqrt{17}\end{aligned}$$
(e) The gradient is $2$, so the vertical distance is $2\sqrt{17}$. By Pythagoras,
$$\begin{aligned}AB&=\sqrt{(\sqrt{17})^2+(2\sqrt{17})^2}\\&=\sqrt{17+68}\\&=\sqrt{85}\end{aligned}$$

Given that $x=-\frac{1}{2}$ is a double root, show that
$$4\left(\frac{c}{a}\right)-16\left(\frac{d}{a}\right)=1$$

answer.worked:
The roots are $-\frac12,-\frac12,\gamma$.
$$\begin{align*}\frac ca&=\frac14-\frac\gamma2-\frac\gamma2=\frac14-\gamma\\-\frac da&=\frac14\gamma\\\frac da&=-\frac\gamma4\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}4\left(\frac ca\right)-16\left(\frac da\right)&=4\left(\frac14-\gamma\right)+4\gamma\\&=1\end{align*}$$

content.prompt:
The cubic equation $x^{3}+2x^{2}+5x-1=0$ has roots $\alpha$, $\beta$ and $\gamma$.
Which cubic equation has roots $\dfrac{-1}{\alpha},\dfrac{-1}{\beta},\dfrac{-1}{\gamma}$?

(A) $x^{3}-5x^{2}-2x+1=0$
(B) $x^{3}-5x^{2}-2x-1=0$
(C) $x^{3}+5x^{2}+2x+1=0$
(D) $x^{3}+5x^{2}-2x+1=0$

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\alpha+\beta+\gamma&=-2\\\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha&=5\\\alpha\beta\gamma&=1\end{align*}$$
For the new roots:
$$\begin{align*}\text{sum}&=-\frac{\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha}{\alpha\beta\gamma}=-5\\\text{pairs}&=\frac{\alpha+\beta+\gamma}{\alpha\beta\gamma}=-2\\\text{product}&=-\frac{1}{\alpha\beta\gamma}=-1\end{align*}$$
The equation is $x^3+5x^2-2x+1=0$. Answer: D.

content.prompt:
The cubic equation $ax^3+bx^2+cx+d=0$ has one root which is equal to the average of the other two roots.
Show that $27a^2d+2b^3=9abc$.

answer.short: With roots $\alpha-\beta,\alpha,\alpha+\beta$: $\alpha=-\dfrac b{3a}$, and substituting into the equation gives $27a^2d+2b^3=9abc$.
answer.worked:
Let the roots be $\alpha-\beta$, $\alpha$ and $\alpha+\beta$.
$$\begin{align*}3\alpha&=-\frac ba\\\alpha&=-\frac b{3a}\end{align*}$$
Since $\alpha$ is a root:
$$\begin{align*}a\left(-\frac b{3a}\right)^3+b\left(-\frac b{3a}\right)^2+c\left(-\frac b{3a}\right)+d&=0\\-\frac{b^3}{27a^2}+\frac{b^3}{9a^2}-\frac{bc}{3a}+d&=0\end{align*}$$
Multiplying by $27a^2$:
$$\begin{align*}-b^3+3b^3-9abc+27a^2d&=0\\27a^2d+2b^3&=9abc\end{align*}$$

content.prompt:
The equation $x^3 - 3x + 1 = 0$ has roots $\alpha$, $\beta$ and $\gamma$.
Find a cubic equation with integer coefficients that has roots $\alpha^2$, $\beta^2$ and $\gamma^2$.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\alpha+\beta+\gamma&=0\\\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha&=-3\\\alpha\beta\gamma&=-1\end{align*}$$
For the new roots:
$$\begin{align*}\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2&=0^2-2(-3)=6\\\alpha^2\beta^2+\beta^2\gamma^2+\gamma^2\alpha^2&=(-3)^2-2(-1)(0)=9\\\alpha^2\beta^2\gamma^2&=(-1)^2=1\end{align*}$$
The equation is $x^3-6x^2+9x-1=0$.

content.prompt: The quartic polynomial $P(x)=x^4+px^3+qx^2+px+1$ has $x=\alpha$ as a double zero.

children.label: i
children.prompt: Show that $\alpha^{-1}$ is also a zero of $P(x)$.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}P\left(\frac1\alpha\right)&=\frac1{\alpha^4}+\frac p{\alpha^3}+\frac q{\alpha^2}+\frac p\alpha+1\\&=\frac{1+p\alpha+q\alpha^2+p\alpha^3+\alpha^4}{\alpha^4}\\&=\frac{P(\alpha)}{\alpha^4}\\&=0\end{align*}$$
So $\alpha^{-1}$ is also a zero.

children.label: ii
children.prompt: Find the fourth root in terms of $\alpha$.

answer.worked:
Let the roots be $\alpha,\alpha,\dfrac1\alpha,\beta$. The product of roots is $1$:
$$\begin{align*}\alpha^2\cdot\frac1\alpha\cdot\beta&=1\\\beta&=\frac1\alpha\end{align*}$$

The roots are $\alpha,\alpha,\dfrac1\alpha,\dfrac1\alpha$.
$$\begin{align*}-p&=2\left(\alpha+\frac1\alpha\right)\\p^2&=4\left(\alpha^2+2+\frac1{\alpha^2}\right)\end{align*}$$
Sum of pairwise products:
$$\begin{align*}q&=\alpha^2+4+\frac1{\alpha^2}\\q-2&=\alpha^2+2+\frac1{\alpha^2}\end{align*}$$
Therefore $p^2=4(q-2)$.

content.prompt:
A circle passing through the origin $O$ is tangent to the hyperbola $xy=1$ at $A$ and intersects the hyperbola again at two distinct points $B$ and $C$.
The co-ordinates of the points $A,B$ and $C$ are $\left(t,\frac{1}{t}\right)$, $\left(t_1,\frac{1}{t_1}\right)$ and $\left(t_2,\frac{1}{t_2}\right)$ respectively.

children.label: ii
children.prompt: Show that the gradient of $BC$ is $-\frac{1}{t_1t_2}$.

answer.worked:
Since the circle passes through the origin, write its equation as:
$$\begin{align*}
x^2+y^2+Dx+Ey&=0
\end{align*}$$
Substitute $y=\frac{1}{x}$:
$$\begin{align*}
x^2+\frac{1}{x^2}+Dx+\frac{E}{x}&=0 \\
x^4+Dx^3+Ex+1&=0
\end{align*}$$
The circle is tangent to the hyperbola at $A$, so $x=t$ is a repeated root. The other roots are $t_1$ and $t_2$. Hence:
$$\begin{align*}
t^2t_1t_2&=1 \\
t_1t_2&=\frac{1}{t^2}
\end{align*}$$
Using part (ii):
$$\begin{align*}
m_{BC}&=-\frac{1}{t_1t_2} \\
&=-t^2
\end{align*}$$
Therefore:
$$\begin{align*}
m_{OA}m_{BC}&=\frac{1}{t^2}(-t^2) \\
&=-1
\end{align*}$$
Hence, $OA$ is perpendicular to $BC$.

content.prompt:
Consider the polynomial $P(x) = x^3 + kx^2 + mx + n$ with distinct zeros $\alpha$, $\beta$ and $\gamma$.
Let $Q(x)$ be a monic polynomial with zeros $\alpha^2$, $\beta^2$ and $\gamma^2$.

answer.worked:
Since $P(x)$ is a monic cubic with roots $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$, it can be factored as:
$$\begin{align*}
P(x) &= (x - \alpha)(x - \beta)(x - \gamma)
\end{align*}$$
Substitute $-x$ into the polynomial:
$$\begin{align*}
P(-x) &= (-x - \alpha)(-x - \beta)(-x - \gamma) \\
&= -(x + \alpha)(x + \beta)(x + \gamma)
\end{align*}$$
Multiply $P(x)$ by $P(-x)$:
$$\begin{align*}
P(x)P(-x) &= -(x - \alpha)(x + \alpha)(x - \beta)(x + \beta)(x - \gamma)(x + \gamma) \\
&= -(x^2 - \alpha^2)(x^2 - \beta^2)(x^2 - \gamma^2)
\end{align*}$$
By definition, $Q(x)$ is the monic polynomial with roots $\alpha^2, \beta^2, \gamma^2$:
$$\begin{align*}
Q(x) &= (x - \alpha^2)(x - \beta^2)(x - \gamma^2)
\end{align*}$$
Substituting $x^2$ into $Q(x)$ gives:
$$\begin{align*}
Q(x^2) &= (x^2 - \alpha^2)(x^2 - \beta^2)(x^2 - \gamma^2) \\
&= -P(x)P(-x)
\end{align*}$$

We expand $-P(x)P(-x)$ algebraically:
$$\begin{align*}
Q(x^2) &= -(x^3 + kx^2 + mx + n)(-x^3 + kx^2 - mx + n) \\
&= (x^3 + kx^2 + mx + n)(x^3 - kx^2 + mx - n)
\end{align*}$$
Expanding this product by grouping even and odd terms:
$$\begin{align*}
Q(x^2) &= ((x^3 + mx) + (kx^2 + n))((x^3 + mx) - (kx^2 + n)) \\
&= (x^3 + mx)^2 - (kx^2 + n)^2 \\
&= (x^6 + 2mx^4 + m^2x^2) - (k^2x^4 + 2knx^2 + n^2) \\
&= x^6 + (2m - k^2)x^4 + (m^2 - 2kn)x^2 - n^2
\end{align*}$$
Replacing $x^2$ with $x$ gives the polynomial $Q(x)$:
$$\begin{align*}
Q(x) &= x^3 - (k^2 - 2m)x^2 + (m^2 - 2kn)x - n^2
\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt:
Consider the polynomial $P(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 - x + 1$ with distinct zeros $\alpha$, $\beta$ and $\gamma$.
By using two applications of the result in part b, or otherwise, show that the polynomial $R(x) = x^3 - 107x^2 + 27x - 1$ has zeros $\alpha^4$, $\beta^4$ and $\gamma^4$.

answer.worked:
For $P(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 - x + 1$, the coefficients are $k = -3$, $m = -1$, and $n = 1$.
Applying the result from part b generates a polynomial $Q(x)$ with roots $\alpha^2, \beta^2, \gamma^2$:
$$\begin{align*}
Q(x) &= x^3 - ((-3)^2 - 2(-1))x^2 + ((-1)^2 - 2(-3)(1))x - 1^2 \\
&= x^3 - (9 + 2)x^2 + (1 + 6)x - 1 \\
&= x^3 - 11x^2 + 7x - 1
\end{align*}$$
To find a polynomial with roots $\alpha^4, \beta^4, \gamma^4$, we apply the transformation a second time to $Q(x)$. The new coefficients are $K = -11$, $M = 7$, and $N = -1$:
$$\begin{align*}
R(x) &= x^3 - (K^2 - 2M)x^2 + (M^2 - 2KN)x - N^2 \\
&= x^3 - ((-11)^2 - 2(7))x^2 + (7^2 - 2(-11)(-1))x - (-1)^2 \\
&= x^3 - (121 - 14)x^2 + (49 - 22)x - 1 \\
&= x^3 - 107x^2 + 27x - 1
\end{align*}$$

children.label: d
children.prompt: By assuming that $\alpha > 0$, and that the magnitude of $\alpha$ is significantly greater than the magnitudes of $\beta$ and $\gamma$, and by considering the sum of zeros of $R(x)$ above, explain why $\alpha^4 \approx 107$.

answer.short: $\alpha^4+\beta^4+\gamma^4=107$. The remaining fourth powers are negligible relative to $\alpha^4$, so $\alpha^4\approx107$.
answer.worked:
The sum of the roots of $R(x)$ is given by the negative coefficient of $x^2$:
$$\begin{align*}
\alpha^4 + \beta^4 + \gamma^4 &= -(-107) = 107
\end{align*}$$
If the magnitude of $\alpha$ is significantly greater than the magnitudes of $\beta$ and $\gamma$ ($|\alpha| > |\beta|$ and $|\alpha| > |\gamma|$), raising these to the fourth power magnifies this difference, making $\beta^4$ and $\gamma^4$ very small relative to $\alpha^4$. Therefore, $\beta^4 + \gamma^4 \approx 0$, which implies:
$$\begin{align*}
\alpha^4 &\approx 107
\end{align*}$$

children.label: e
children.prompt: Hence find an approximation for $\alpha$ to $2$ decimal places and verify it is a good approximation for a zero of $P(x)$.

answer.short: $\alpha\approx3.22$ and $P(3.22)\approx0.061$, which is close to zero.
answer.worked:
Solving for $\alpha$ (taking the positive root as given $\alpha > 0$):
$$\begin{align*}
\alpha &\approx \sqrt[4]{107} \\
&\approx 3.22
\end{align*}$$
To verify this is a good approximation, we substitute $x = 3.22$ back into the original polynomial $P(x)$:
$$\begin{align*}
P(3.22) &= (3.22)^3 - 3(3.22)^2 - 3.22 + 1 \\
&\approx 33.386 - 31.105 - 3.22 + 1 \\
&\approx 0.061
\end{align*}$$
Since $P(3.22)$ is very close to $0$, $3.22$ is a very good approximation for the root $\alpha$.

content.prompt: Two roots of $x^3+mx^2-3x-18=0$ are equal and rational. Find $m$.

answer.worked:
Let the roots be $\alpha,\alpha,\beta$.

Sum of roots:
$$2\alpha+\beta=-m\qquad(1)$$
Product of roots:
$$\alpha^2\beta=18\qquad(2)$$
Sum of products taken two at a time:
$$\alpha^2+2\alpha\beta=-3\qquad(3)$$
From (2), $\beta=\frac{18}{\alpha^2}$. Substituting into (3):
$$\begin{align*}\alpha^2+2\alpha\left(\frac{18}{\alpha^2}\right)&=-3\\\alpha^3+3\alpha+36&=0\end{align*}$$
Test factors of 36. For $P(t)=t^3+3t+36$,
$$P(-3)=-27-9+36=0.$$
By long division,
$$\alpha^3+3\alpha+36=(\alpha+3)(\alpha^2-3\alpha+12).$$
For the quadratic factor,
$$\Delta=(-3)^2-4(1)(12)=-39<0.$$
Thus $\alpha=-3$ is the only rational root.
$$\beta=\frac{18}{(-3)^2}=2.$$
Using (1):
$$\begin{align*}-3-3+2&=-m\\-4&=-m\\m&=4\end{align*}$$

inlines.text: Find the zeroes of the polynomial
given that one of them is the product of the other two.

answer.worked:
The roots are $\alpha,\beta,\alpha\beta$. Their sums and products give
$$\begin{align*}
\alpha+\beta+\alpha\beta&=\frac{13}{2}\\
\alpha\beta+\alpha^2\beta+\alpha\beta^2&=11\\
\alpha\beta(1+\alpha+\beta)&=11\\
\alpha^2\beta^2&=4\\
\alpha\beta&=\pm2.
\end{align*}$$
Consider $\alpha\beta=2$:
$$\begin{align*}
\alpha+\beta+2&=\frac{13}{2}\\
\alpha+\beta&=\frac92.
\end{align*}$$
Check the sum of products:
$$2\left(1+\frac92\right)=11\quad\checkmark$$
If $\alpha\beta=-2$, the sum of roots gives $\alpha+\beta=\frac{17}{2}$, but
$$-2\left(1+\frac{17}{2}\right)=-19\ne11.$$
Reject $\alpha\beta=-2$. Thus $\alpha+\beta=\frac92$ and $\alpha\beta=2$. The two roots $\alpha,\beta$ satisfy
$$\begin{align*}
t^2-\frac92t+2&=0\\
2t^2-9t+4&=0\\
(2t-1)(t-4)&=0.
\end{align*}$$
Hence $\{\alpha,\beta\}=\{\frac12,4\}$ and $\alpha\beta=2$. The zeroes are $\frac12,2,4$.

content.prompt: If one root of the equation $x^3-bx^2+cx-d=0$ is equal to the product of the other two, show that $(c+d)^2=d(b+a)^2$, where $a=1$.

answer.short: Writing the roots as $\alpha,\beta,\alpha\beta$ gives $b=\alpha+\beta+\alpha\beta$, $c=\alpha\beta(1+\alpha+\beta)$ and $d=\alpha^2\beta^2$. Hence $(c+d)^2=d(1+b)^2=d(b+a)^2$, since $a=1$.
answer.worked:
Let the zeroes be $\alpha,\beta,\alpha\beta$.

Sum of roots:
$$\alpha+\beta+\alpha\beta=b.$$
Sum of products of pairs of roots:
$$\begin{aligned}\alpha\beta+\alpha\beta^2+\alpha^2\beta&=c\\\alpha\beta(1+\beta+\alpha)&=c.\end{aligned}$$
Product of roots:
$$\alpha^2\beta^2=d.$$
Now
$$\begin{aligned}(c+d)^2&=c^2+2cd+d^2\\&=\alpha^2\beta^2(1+\beta+\alpha)^2+2\alpha^3\beta^3(1+\beta+\alpha)+\alpha^4\beta^4\\&=\alpha^2\beta^2\big[(1+\beta+\alpha)^2+2\alpha\beta(1+\beta+\alpha)+\alpha^2\beta^2\big].\end{aligned}$$
Recognising the perfect square,
$$\begin{aligned}(c+d)^2&=\alpha^2\beta^2\big((1+\alpha+\beta)+\alpha\beta\big)^2\\&=d(1+b)^2\\&=d(a+b)^2,\end{aligned}$$
since $a=1$, as required.

content.prompt: Find the zeroes of $x^4-3x^3-8x^2+12x+16$ if they are $\alpha$, $2\alpha$, $\beta$, and $2\beta$.

answer.worked:
Sum of roots:
$$\begin{align*}3\alpha+3\beta&=3\\\alpha+\beta&=1\end{align*}$$
Product of roots:
$$\begin{align*}4\alpha^2\beta^2&=16\\\alpha^2\beta^2&=4\end{align*}$$
Solving simultaneously:
$$\begin{align*}\alpha^2(1-\alpha)^2&=4\\\alpha(1-\alpha)&=\pm2\end{align*}$$
Consider two cases.

For $\alpha(1-\alpha)=2$:
$$\begin{align*}\alpha^2-\alpha+2&=0\\\Delta&=1-8\\&=-7<0\end{align*}$$
This case has no real solution. It also fails the quartic's coefficients: here $\alpha\beta=2$, so the sum of pairwise products would be
$$\begin{align*}2\alpha^2+9\alpha\beta+2\beta^2&=2(\alpha+\beta)^2+5\alpha\beta\\&=2(1)^2+5(2)\\&=12,\end{align*}$$
whereas the coefficient of $x^2$ requires $-8$.

For $\alpha(1-\alpha)=-2$:
$$\begin{align*}\alpha^2-\alpha-2&=0\\(\alpha+1)(\alpha-2)&=0\\\alpha&=-1\text{ or }2\end{align*}$$
If $\alpha=-1$, then $\beta=2$. If $\alpha=2$, then $\beta=-1$; these give the same four zeroes.

The zeroes are $-1,-2,2,4$.

Check:
$$\begin{align*}(x+1)(x+2)(x-2)(x-4)&=(x^2-x-2)(x^2-2x-8)\\&=x^4-3x^3-8x^2+12x+16.\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: The polynomial equation $x^4+px^3+qx^2+rx+s=0$ has two roots that sum to zero, and another two roots that are reciprocals of each other. Show that:

answer.worked:
Let the roots be $\alpha,-\alpha,\beta,\dfrac1\beta$.

The product of the roots gives
$$\begin{aligned}s&=\alpha(-\alpha)\beta\frac1\beta\\s&=-\alpha^2.\end{aligned}$$
The sum of the pairwise products gives
$$\begin{aligned}q&=-\alpha^2+\alpha\beta+\frac\alpha\beta-\alpha\beta-\frac\alpha\beta+1\\q&=-\alpha^2+1\\q&=1+s.\end{aligned}$$

Let the roots be $\alpha,-\alpha,\beta,\dfrac1\beta$. Their sum and product give
$$\begin{aligned}\beta+\frac1\beta&=-p,\\-\alpha^2&=s.\end{aligned}$$
The sum of the triple products is $-r$:
$$\begin{aligned}-r&=-\alpha^2\beta-\frac{\alpha^2}{\beta}-\alpha+\alpha\\-r&=-\alpha^2\left(\beta+\frac1\beta\right)\\-r&=s(-p)\\-r&=-sp\\r&=ps.\end{aligned}$$

content.prompt: Find the value(s) of $k$ if the quadratic equation $x^2-(k+2)x+k+1=0$ has:

answer.worked:
Let the roots be $r$ and $2r$.
$$\begin{aligned}3r&=k+2\\r&=\frac{k+2}{3}\\2r^2&=k+1\\2\left(\frac{k+2}{3}\right)^2&=k+1\\2k^2+8k+8&=9k+9\\2k^2-k-1&=0\\(2k+1)(k-1)&=0\\k&=-\frac12\text{ or }1\end{aligned}$$

content.prompt: If the roots of the equation $x^2+px+q=0$ are consecutive numbers, show that $p^2=4q+1$.

answer.worked:
Let the roots be $\alpha$ and $\alpha+1$.

Sum of roots:
$$2\alpha+1=-p\qquad(1)$$
Product of roots:
$$\alpha^2+\alpha=q\qquad(2)$$
Rearrange (1): $\alpha=\frac{-p-1}{2}$. Substitute into (2):
$$\begin{aligned}\left(\frac{-p-1}{2}\right)^2+\frac{-p-1}{2}&=q\\\frac{p^2+2p+1}{4}+\frac{-2p-2}{4}&=q\\p^2-1&=4q\\p^2&=4q+1\end{aligned}$$

content.prompt: The polynomial equation $x^4+ax^3+bx^2+cx+d=0$ has roots $\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Hence, show that $x^4-3x^3+5x^2+4x-1=0$ cannot have four real roots.

answer.short: The sum of the squares of the roots is $(-3)^2-2(5)=-1<0$, which is impossible if all four roots are real.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2+\delta^2&=a^2-2b\\&=(-3)^2-2(5)\\&=-1<0\end{aligned}$$
If all four roots were real, each square would be non-negative, so their sum would be non-negative. Therefore the equation cannot have four real roots.

content.prompt: The polynomial $P(x)=x^4+ax^3+bx^2+cx+d$ has two zeroes that are opposites and two zeroes that are reciprocals. Show that $b=1+d$ and $c=ad$.

answer.worked:
Let the roots be $\alpha,-\alpha,\beta,\dfrac1\beta$, where $\beta\ne0$.

Sum of roots:
$$\beta+\frac1\beta=-a\qquad(1)$$
Sum of products two at a time:
$$\begin{align*}-\alpha^2+\alpha\beta+\frac\alpha\beta-\alpha\beta-\frac\alpha\beta+1&=b\\-\alpha^2+1&=b\qquad(2)\end{align*}$$
Sum of products three at a time:
$$\begin{align*}-\alpha^2\beta-\frac{\alpha^2}{\beta}+\alpha-\alpha&=-c\\-\alpha^2\left(\beta+\frac1\beta\right)&=-c\qquad(3)\end{align*}$$
Product of roots:
$$-\alpha^2=d\qquad(4)$$
Substitute (4) into (2):
$$\begin{align*}d+1&=b\\b&=1+d.\end{align*}$$
Substitute (1) and (4) into (3):
$$\begin{align*}d(-a)&=-c\\-ad&=-c\\c&=ad.\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: Let $x^3+5x-1=0$ have roots $\alpha$, $\beta$ and $\gamma$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Hence, explain why the graph of $y=x^3+5x-1$ cannot have 3 $x$-intercepts.

answer.short: If all three roots were real, their squares would have a non-negative sum. Since the sum is $-10$, the roots cannot all be real, so the graph cannot have 3 $x$-intercepts.
answer.worked: A cubic has three roots, counting multiplicity. If all three were real, $\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2\geq0$. Part a gives $\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2=-10$, so the roots cannot all be real. Hence the graph cannot have 3 $x$-intercepts.

[Pedagogy audit v2 · Bridge] The step from routine quartic questions to the quartic proofs is large, because naming constrained roots and using the three-at-a-time sums is not practised for quartics. Add a scaffolded quartic proof between them.
Proposed question: The polynomial $P(x)=x^4-6x^3+bx^2+cx+d$ has zeroes $t$, $-t$, $u$ and $v$.
a) Show that $c=6t^2$.
b) Hence show that $c^2+6bc+36d=0$.
Answers: a) The sum of the roots gives $u+v=6$, and the triple-product relation gives $-t^2(u+v)=-c$, so $c=6t^2$.; b) The pair and product relations give $uv=b+t^2$ and $d=-t^2uv$. With $t^2=\dfrac c6$, this gives $36d=-6bc-c^2$, so $c^2+6bc+36d=0$.

flags.note:
[Pedagogy audit v2 · New teaching] Questions 15 and 18 ask for a quadratic whose roots are functions of α and β, but no teaching shows how to build it from the new sum and product. Add a worked example after the related-roots example.
Worked example: Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be the roots of $x^2-5x+3=0$. Find the quadratic equation whose roots are $\dfrac1\alpha$ and $\dfrac1\beta$.
$$\begin{aligned}\alpha+\beta&=5\\\alpha\beta&=3\end{aligned}$$
Let the new quadratic be $x^2+\frac ba x+\frac ca=0$.

Sum of new roots:
$$\begin{aligned}\frac1\alpha+\frac1\beta&=-\frac ba\\\frac{\alpha+\beta}{\alpha\beta}&=-\frac ba\\\frac53&=-\frac ba\end{aligned}$$
Product of new roots:
$$\begin{aligned}\frac1\alpha\cdot\frac1\beta&=\frac ca\\\frac1{\alpha\beta}&=\frac ca\\\frac13&=\frac ca\end{aligned}$$
So
$$\begin{aligned}x^2-\frac53x+\frac13&=0\\\color{#ef6068}{3\times}\left(x^2-\frac53x+\frac13\right)&=\color{#ef6068}{3\times}\,0\\3x^2-5x+1&=0\end{aligned}$$
Guided practice:
Proposed question: Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be the roots of $2x^2-6x+3=0$. Find the quadratic equation whose roots are:
a) $\dfrac1\alpha$ and $\dfrac1\beta$
b) $\alpha^2$ and $\beta^2$
c) $\alpha-2$ and $\beta-2$
Answers: a) $3x^2-6x+2=0$.; b) $4x^2-24x+9=0$.; c) $2x^2+2x-1=0$.

flags.note:
[Pedagogy audit v2 · New teaching] Students are asked to explain why roots are not real from a negative α²+β², but the lesson never states this idea. Add one sentence after the identity.
Worked example: Show that $x^2-2x+3=0$ cannot have two real roots.
Let the roots be $\alpha$ and $\beta$.
$$\begin{aligned}\alpha+\beta&=-\frac ba=2\\\alpha\beta&=\frac ca=3\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\alpha^2+\beta^2&=(\alpha+\beta)^2-2\alpha\beta\\&=2^2-2(3)\\&=-2<0\end{aligned}$$
The square of a real number is non-negative. If both roots were real, $\alpha^2+\beta^2$ would be non-negative.

Therefore the equation cannot have two real roots.
Guided practice:
Proposed question: Show that each equation cannot have two real roots.
a) $x^2+2x+5=0$
b) $3x^2-2x+4=0$
c) $2x^2+5=0$
Answers: a) $\alpha^2+\beta^2=(-2)^2-2(5)=-6<0$, so the roots cannot both be real.; b) $\alpha^2+\beta^2=\left(\dfrac23\right)^2-2\left(\dfrac43\right)=-\dfrac{20}{9}<0$, so the roots cannot both be real.; c) $\alpha^2+\beta^2=0^2-2\left(\dfrac52\right)=-5<0$, so the roots cannot both be real.

[Pedagogy audit v2 · New teaching] The cubic questions on kα and 1/α need a worked example of forming x³−S₁x²+S₂x−S₃=0 from the new roots' sums. Nothing in the lesson teaches it.
Worked example: Let $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ be the roots of $x^3-5x^2+4x-3=0$. Find the cubic equation whose roots are $\dfrac1\alpha,\dfrac1\beta$ and $\dfrac1\gamma$.
For the original roots,
$$\begin{align*}\alpha+\beta+\gamma&=5\\\alpha\beta+\alpha\gamma+\beta\gamma&=4\\\alpha\beta\gamma&=3.\end{align*}$$
For the new roots $\frac1\alpha,\frac1\beta,\frac1\gamma$,
$$\begin{align*}\frac1\alpha+\frac1\beta+\frac1\gamma&=\frac{\beta\gamma+\alpha\gamma+\alpha\beta}{\alpha\beta\gamma}=\frac43,\\\frac1{\alpha\beta}+\frac1{\alpha\gamma}+\frac1{\beta\gamma}&=\frac{\gamma+\beta+\alpha}{\alpha\beta\gamma}=\frac53,\\\frac1{\alpha\beta\gamma}&=\frac13.\end{align*}$$
A monic cubic with root sum $S_1$, sum of pairwise products $S_2$ and root product $S_3$ has equation $x^3-S_1x^2+S_2x-S_3=0$.
$$\begin{align*}x^3-\frac43x^2+\frac53x-\frac13&=0\\\color{#ef6068}{3\times}\left(x^3-\frac43x^2+\frac53x-\frac13\right)&=\color{#ef6068}{3\times}\,0\\3x^3-4x^2+5x-1&=0\end{align*}$$
Guided practice:
Proposed question: Complete the following.
a) Let $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ be the roots of $x^3+3x^2-6x-2=0$.
Find the cubic equation whose roots are $-2\alpha,-2\beta$ and $-2\gamma$.
b) Let $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ be the roots of $2x^3-4x^2+5x+1=0$.
Find the cubic equation whose roots are $\frac1\alpha,\frac1\beta,\frac1\gamma$.
c) Let $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ be the roots of $x^3-4x+6=0$.
Find the cubic equation whose roots are $\frac1\alpha,\frac1\beta,\frac1\gamma$.
Answers: a) $x^3-6x^2-24x+16=0$.; b) $x^3+5x^2-4x+2=0$.; c) $6x^3-4x^2+1=0$.

entries.description:
Consider this polynomial.
P(x) = (x − 2)(x − 3)(x − 5)(x − 7) = x⁴ − 17x³ + 110x² − 247x + 210
The coefficients of the expanded polynomial are: 1, −17, 101, −247, 210
These must come from 2, 3, 5, 7. But can we get them quickly without expanding?

entries.description:
If we can find a formula relating the coefficients and the zeroes, we can factorise and expand polynomials very quickly.
Let’s start with a quadratic function f(x) = ax² + bx + c,
The zeroes, or roots, of the function are when f(x) = ………
This corresponds to the ……-intercepts of the function.

To find the zeroes, we can use the quadratic formula:
x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac))/(2a)

entries.description:
Let roots be α and 2α.
Sum of roots:
α + 2α = −2
3α = −2
α = −2/3

∴ roots are −2/3 and −4/3

Product of roots:
α(2α) = −5p
2α² = −5p
p = −2α²/5
  = [−2(−2/3)²]/5
  = −8/45

Let roots be α, α + 1
Sum of roots: 2α + 1 = −p   (1)
Product of roots: α² + α = q   (2)
Rearrange (1): α = (−p − 1)/2, Sub into (2)
((−p − 1)/2)² + (−p − 1)/2 = q

p² − 1 = 4q
p² = 4q + 1

entries.description:
Harder questions require you to prove general statements about polynomials.
There is no step-by-step procedure for these questions, but it is helpful to:
• Clearly define the roots using the restrictions.
• Begin by writing out the sums and products of roots formulas.
• Use the sum equations and product equations first, as they are most simple.
• Use simultaneous equations to show the required statement.
• It is often easier if you do not find expressions for individual roots.

from (2), β = 18/α² sub into (3)

entries.description:
Supplied worked proof: Let zeroes be α, β, αβ.
Sum of roots: α + β + αβ = b.
Sum of product of pairs of roots: αβ + αβ² + α²β = c.
αβ(1 + β + α) = c.
Product of roots: α²β² = d.
LHS = (c + d)²
= c² + 2cd + d²
= α²β²(1 + β + α)² + 2α³β³(1 + β + α) + α⁴β⁴
= α²β²[(1 + β + α)² + 2αβ(1 + β + α) + α²β²].

= α²β²((1 + α + β) + αβ)²
= d(a + b)² as required.

entries.description:

Sum of roots: 2α + 2β = A (1).
Sum of product of pairs of roots: αβ + β(α + β) + α(α + β) = 0 (2).
Product of roots: αβ(α + β) = −3A (3).
Rearrange (1): α + β = A/2, sub into (2).
αβ + β(A/2) + α(A/2) = 0
αβ + (A/2)(α + β) = 0
αβ + A²/4 = 0
αβ = −A²/4.
Sub value of α + β and αβ into (3).
−(A²/4)(A/2) = −3A
−A³/8 = −3A
A² = 24
A = √24
A = 2√6.
